title: Pool Pre-Shot Routine: 5 Steps to More Consistent Shots
description: Build a simple pre-shot routine in pool: five easy steps, why the pause matters, and three drills to help you miss less and shoot more consistently.
body:
Watch any top pro at the table and you will notice something: they do the exact same thing before every shot. Same pause, same steps, same rhythm. That is not superstition. It is a pre-shot routine, and it is one of the fastest ways for a beginner to stop missing easy balls.

What is a pre-shot routine?

A pre-shot routine is a short, repeatable set of steps you follow every time, from the moment you stand up and look at the table to the moment you strike the cue ball. The goal is simple: make your good shots happen on purpose instead of by luck.

Coaches and instructors commonly describe it the same way: pick a routine, use it on easy shots and hard shots alike, and your body learns the pattern. When nerves show up, the routine gives your mind a familiar job to do.

A simple five-step routine

Here is a beginner-friendly version you can start using tonight. Feel free to tweak it, but keep the order the same every time.

  1. Stand and decide. Look at the table from behind the shot, not while bent over it. Choose the ball, the pocket and where you want the cue ball to end up. (See our position play guide for help with that last part.)
  2. Find the line. Picture the path the cue ball must travel. If you are working on aiming, our ghost ball aiming guide shows an easy way to find the contact point.
  3. Chalk and step in. Chalk the tip, then walk into the shot along that line so your body ends up lined up with it. Set your feet and bridge hand.
  4. Warm up with practice strokes. Take a few smooth practice strokes that match the speed of the real shot. Use small, gentle strokes for soft shots and fuller ones for firm shots. Look back and forth between the cue ball and your target.
  5. Pause, then shoot. Pause briefly with the tip near the cue ball, then make a smooth final stroke and stay down until the ball has been struck and the cue ball is rolling.

Why the pause matters

Many instructors point to a short pause at the end of the backswing or just before the final stroke. It gives your eyes, brain and arm a moment to agree on the shot. Rushing from the last practice stroke straight into the hit is a common beginner habit, and it often leads to jerky strokes and wandering aim.

Check your stance and comfort

A routine only works if your setup is comfortable and balanced. Basic fundamentals checklists, including one used by a university billiards program, ask players to chalk and check the tip, set their eyes over the aiming line and place their back foot on or near that line. If your knees, back or shoulders feel strained, adjust your stance before you shoot. For more help, read our guide to building a solid bridge and stance.

The golden rule: stand up and restart

Here is the habit that separates steady players from streaky ones. If you are down on the shot and something feels off, maybe you doubt the line or your hand slipped, do not shoot anyway. Stand up, take a breath, and start the routine again. It costs five seconds, and it can save you a whole rack.

Three ways to practice your routine

  • The straight-in drill. Place the cue ball and an object ball in a straight line with a pocket. Use your full routine on ten shots in a row. Count how many go in.
  • The slow-motion rack. Play a rack of 8-ball alone, and never skip a step, even on a gimme. Easy shots are where habits are built.
  • The pressure shot. Make a rule: if you miss, start the drill over. A little pressure shows you whether your routine holds up when it matters.

Want more ideas? Our solo pool drills are a great place to build the routine into your practice sessions.

Watch the pros do it

The best way to see this in action is to watch for it. The Mosconi Cup runs Nov. 27-30 at the Caribe Royale in Orlando, and it is a perfect chance to study how elite players behave at the table under pressure. Notice how each player has a recognizable rhythm: the walk-in, the practice strokes, the pause, the shot. Check our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub for teams, how to watch and results, and the pro events calendar for what is coming next.

Quick recap

  • Pick one routine and use it on every shot, easy or hard.
  • Decide first, then chalk, step in, practice stroke, pause, shoot.
  • Match your practice strokes to the speed of the real shot.
  • If anything feels wrong, stand up and restart.

Your routine does not need to look like anyone else's. It just needs to be yours, and the same every time. Try it at your next session and let us know whether you notice more balls dropping.
